description: Hi! We’re Alvin & Tiffany, frontend developers from Malaysia. We’re building the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser: an interactive site comparing Moon south-pole landing sites using sunlight, Earth visibility, 3D terrain & NASA data. Looing for Data/Python, UI/UX, storytelling/video & space enthusiasts!
summary: CLPS Lunar Mission Browser is a free web app for comparing lunar south pole landing sites and dates. Pick a site and a date range and it shows, from real NASA terrain and ephemeris data, when the site has sunlight for power, when it can see Earth for direct communication, the longest darkness a battery must survive, and the best window to land. It answers in plain words first, then offers a horizon panorama, timelines, a side-by-side comparison of sites and a 3D view of the LOLA terrain with real shadows. When a launch slips, mission planners, educators and the public can re-check new dates and sites in minutes instead of running specialist tools. The model is checked against 1,022 real LRO photos and calls sunlight or shadow right in 99.3% of the cases that can tell. Four games built on the same real data let students learn the south pole by playing.
details:
What it does

CLPS Lunar Mission Browser answers the first questions every lunar south pole mission asks: when will this site have sunlight for power, when can it see Earth to talk home, how long is the longest darkness a battery must survive, and when is the best time to land? Pick one of 14 sites (Artemis candidate regions, the IM-1 and IM-2 landing sites, the VIPER mission area, Shackleton's rim and its permanently shadowed floor) or drop a pin anywhere south of 82°S, choose your dates, and the app answers in plain words first. One click away are the details: a 360° horizon panorama with the Sun's and Earth's paths, a table of windows with both sunlight and Earth in view (CSV export), a solar panel and battery calculator, a mast-height planner, a year-long search for the best landing dates, a side-by-side comparison of sites, and a 3D view of the real terrain with shadows that move over time.

How it works

A Python pipeline uses NASA NAIF SPICE kernels (DE440) to compute the Sun's and Earth's positions every hour, and ray-casts each site's horizon every 0.1° of azimuth out to 300 km over NASA Goddard's LOLA elevation maps (10 m near each site, coarser farther out), for observers from 2 m to 50 m high. The browser does the rest: a Web Worker turns those horizons into sunlight, Earth visibility, metrics and an hour-by-hour battery simulation, so a new site or date updates instantly, with no server and no sign-in.

How we checked it

Our ephemeris agrees with JPL Horizons to within 0.00001°. Across 1,022 LRO Wide Angle Camera photos from 2009–2011, the app calls a site sunlit or in shadow right in 99.3% of the cases clear enough to tell, and the Plan view lets anyone compare a real LRO photo with the model. 66 automated tests cover the math.

Impact

When a launch slips, mission planners can re-check sites and dates in minutes instead of running specialist tools. Educators and the public get a six-step guided tour, a help icon on every section, and four games built on the same real data (Survive the lunar night, Daily landing challenge, Photo quiz, Outrun the shadows), so students learn why the south pole is both attractive and hard. The IM-2 Athena site is included: that mission ended about a day after the lander came down on its side in a crater, a reminder of how much terrain and sunlight matter.

What makes it creative

Hand control lets you wave an open hand at your webcam to move time and watch the shadows sweep across the terrain (the video never leaves your browser). "Listen" turns a site's skyline into sound, and the 3D view can make an Earth postcard of the next moment Earth rises over a site's skyline.

Tools

TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, d3-scale, CesiumJS (3D), MediaPipe (hand tracking) and Vitest; Python with SpiceyPy, NumPy, SciPy, rasterio and pyproj for the data pipeline. Hosted on Vercel. It works on phones.

Factors we considered

Accuracy and honesty: every site is marked as an exact published point or a representative point for a region, all times are UTC, and the Method page states the limits. Newcomers and experts: plain answers first, expert panels folded away. Accessibility: keyboard and screen-reader support, checked with axe-core. Speed: 3D and hand tracking load only when used. Privacy: no accounts, no uploads. Open data: every source is credited on the Credits page.

Use of SI

We used Claude (Anthropic), through Claude Code, as a coding assistant for the app, the data pipeline, the tests and the docs; the team chose the features and checked the results. The demo's voice-over is Microsoft neural text-to-speech; the video carries a visible SI watermark and SI metadata. Every piece of AI-assisted work is logged in AI_USAGE.md in the repository.
